newsitem.title: USA: New NYC agency would not give comptroller any say.
newsitem.headline: New NYC agency would not give comptroller any say.

text.p: New York City's plan for a new infrastructure agency, which it proposed to sidestep the debt limit, is "problematic" partly as it knocks out any role for the comptroller, a deputy city comptroller said on Monday.
This would be a striking departure from the current practice, as the city comptroller now is required to approve all of the city's debt offerings, along with the mayor.
"It's problematic in some senses," explained Richard Halverson, a deputy comptroller.

A spokesman for the city comptroller has said that while Alan Hevesi is open to the plan, he thinks it should have the same sorts of checks and balances between the mayor and the comptroller that the city's general obligation debt now has.

Any new infrastructure authority would have to be approved by both the state legislature and the governor. There has been speculation that the Giuliani Administration will submit its bill after the November 5 elections, when Gov. George Pataki has said he plans to call a special session to deal with the changes required by the federal welfare bill.
A spokesman for Mayor Rudolph Giuliani was not immediately available to comment.

New York City, which is one of the largest sellers in the municipal market with about $30 billion of debt outstanding, is expected to hit the $33 billion limit set by the constitution in the next year or two.

But officials with both the city and state comptrollers reacted coolly to the new plan, saying more discussion was needed, while the MAC board, which had been expected to informally back the idea, instead straddled the fence.
"We're not comfortable or uncomfortable," said Edward Regan, the MAC chairman, at its annual meeting, though he added that he was speaking for himself.
The MAC was set up in 1975 to handle the city's debt crisis, and Regan, a former state comptroller, promised to keep the board advised of developments.

Deputy city comptroller Halverson did not predict that Hevesi would reject the Giuliani Administration's current plan, saying only the comptroller will respond to the innovative proposal and forecasting it would be widely discussed.

Noting it was "not characteristic" as no other authority excludes the comptroller, he that added the mayor's plan was broadly written, and evidently would let the new infrastructure agency refund the debt of lots of agencies.
Further, the bill as it now stands does not limit the agency to drawing solely upon income tax revenues, he noted.

While the state comptroller's deputy, Rosemary Scanlon, said she had yet to see the draft proposed by the Giuliani Administration, she noted this monitor was concerned about who would be in charge and who would be making the decisions.

Other issues she focused on included whether there would be a debt limit, whether the city had presented a full range of options instead of focusing only on the new agency, and whether there was enough revenue to support the new debt.

"If you're taking away from the personal income tax revenues, which are supporting the operating debt, and you are not providing for that money amount of elsewhere. In other words, it hasn't really been dealt with."
Scanlon's concern mirrored a question raised by one representative on the MAC board, Robert Price, the president of Price Communication.

Quentin Spector, the MAC's executive director, said the city plans for its debt service to rise to 19 percent of local revenues from the 13 percent to 14 percent level seen in the past few years, noting it is anxious to avoid any bigger rise.

While the city dropped a plan to use the agency to issue debt for mass transit, it now wants to use the authority to raise $11 billion to $17 billion for building roads, bridges and schools, he said. The amount of debt that could be issued might be limited to two to three times coverage.
